promptText: Integration tests sit in the middle of the test pyramid rather than at the base. What specifically makes them cost more than unit tests, and what should that cost lead you to do?
options: They exercise real collaborators (a real DB connection, Spring context, or container) instead of mocks, so booting that infrastructure takes hundreds of milliseconds to seconds per test — meaning you should keep this layer smaller and reserve it for the seams that actually matter.
They require writing more assertions per test than unit tests do, so they take longer to author even though they run just as fast once written.
They must always run against a full @SpringBootTest context, so the only way to control cost is to delete tests once the suite grows too large.
They are inherently more likely to be flaky than unit tests, so their added cost comes from re-running them multiple times until they pass.
explanation: Booting a real Spring context or Docker container costs real wall-clock time per test; the chapter's guidance is to 'integration-test the seams, not the logic,' not that more assertions or full contexts are inherently required.

promptText: The chapter calls reaching for @SpringBootTest by default 'the single most common way an integration suite becomes slow enough that developers stop running it locally.' What's the recommended alternative, and why does it work?
options: Use the narrowest test slice (e.g., @DataJpaTest, @WebMvcTest) that loads only the beans relevant to the layer under test, since @SpringBootTest boots every bean and auto-configuration in the entire application.
Keep using @SpringBootTest everywhere but reduce the number of test methods per class, since slice annotations only affect method count, not context size.
Replace @SpringBootTest with unit tests everywhere, since Spring context loading should never happen in a test suite.
Use @SpringBootTest but mark it @DirtiesContext so Spring skips loading auto-configurations it doesn't recognize.
explanation: Test slices load only the beans relevant to one layer, keeping most integration tests fast; @SpringBootTest should be reserved for tests that genuinely need the whole wiring.

promptText: A repository integration test is annotated @Transactional so Spring rolls back changes after each test method. The chapter warns this safety net has a specific blind spot. What is it?
options: It doesn't help if the code under test opens its own transaction (e.g., via REQUIRES_NEW) or if the test is asserting against something outside the database transaction entirely, like a Kafka topic.
It doesn't help because @Transactional only works with @WebMvcTest, never with @DataJpaTest or @SpringBootTest.
It doesn't help because rollback only reverts INSERT statements, not UPDATE or DELETE statements.
It doesn't help because Spring only rolls back the transaction if the test method throws an exception.
explanation: A REQUIRES_NEW propagation commits independently of the outer rollback, and side effects like a published Kafka message are never part of the database transaction, so rollback cannot undo either.

promptText: In a JUnit 5 Testcontainers setup, what's the practical difference between a non-static @Container field and a static @Container field?
options: A non-static field starts and stops fresh for every test method (strong isolation, slower); a static field starts once and is shared across all methods in the class (faster, but needs its own state cleanup between tests).
A non-static field is only usable with @DataJpaTest, while a static field is only usable with @SpringBootTest.
A non-static field requires Docker-in-Docker in CI, while a static field works without any Docker daemon at all.
There is no functional difference; static only affects whether the field can be accessed from a @BeforeAll method.
explanation: Non-static containers give per-test isolation at a real speed cost, while static (per-class) containers are shared and faster but push the burden of state cleanup between tests onto the author.

promptText: How does a consumer-driven contract (Pact's model) differ from a provider-driven/schema-first approach, and what's the key benefit of the consumer-driven model?
options: In consumer-driven contracts, the consumer specifies exactly what it expects and reads, and the provider verifies against that; this means a provider can freely evolve unused parts of its API without failing verification, unlike schema diffing which flags any change.
In consumer-driven contracts, the provider dictates the exact contract and the consumer must implement a matching client, which guarantees the consumer never breaks even if it ignores the schema.
Consumer-driven and provider-driven contracts are functionally identical; the only difference is which team's CI server hosts the Pact Broker.
Consumer-driven contracts require both services to be deployed simultaneously so the consumer can record real traffic against the live provider.
explanation: Because the contract only encodes fields the consumer actually reads, providers can add fields or evolve unused surface area without triggering false-positive failures — a more actionable signal than full schema diffing.

promptText: The chapter lists 'relying on a fixed port instead of Testcontainers' dynamically mapped port' as a common CI failure mode. Why does Testcontainers map to a random host port in the first place, and what happens if you fight that by hardcoding it?
options: Testcontainers randomizes the host port so concurrent test runs/containers of the same image don't collide; hardcoding the port re-introduces exactly the collision flakiness the random mapping was designed to prevent.

Testcontainers randomizes the host port purely for security, to prevent other processes on the CI runner from connecting to the test database; hardcoding it has no functional effect on test reliability.
Testcontainers randomizes the host port because Docker requires all container ports to be ephemeral by default; hardcoding it simply makes tests run faster with no downside.
Testcontainers randomizes the host port only in local development, never in CI, so hardcoding a port is safe as long as it's only done in the CI configuration.
explanation: Reading the port back via getMappedPort()/getJdbcUrl() matters because concurrent runs — parallel CI jobs or multiple containers of the same image — would otherwise collide on a fixed port.

promptText: A team's repository tests pass against H2 in Postgres-compatibility mode but fail in production. The chapter's anecdote traces this to a specific class of bug. What is the mechanism?
options: H2 approximates Postgres SQL but silently diverges on dialect-specific features like JSONB columns, array types, and window functions, so a query using a Postgres-specific operator can pass on H2 while a real type mismatch goes undetected until it runs against real Postgres.
H2 and Postgres are byte-for-byte compatible at the JDBC driver level, so any divergence is caused exclusively by network latency differences between an in-memory database and a networked one.
H2 tests fail in production only because H2 cannot run inside Docker, so any test suite using H2 must also separately run against Testcontainers just to compile.
H2 diverges from Postgres only in transaction isolation levels, never in SQL syntax or dialect-specific types, so the fix is always to add @Transactional to the failing test.
explanation: This mirrors the chapter's explicit anecdote — a Postgres-specific JSONB operator's type mismatch was silently ignored by H2 and only surfaced against the real dialect via Testcontainers.

promptText: A developer wires up @DataJpaTest with a Testcontainers PostgreSQLContainer and @DynamicPropertySource, but the test still appears to run against an embedded database instead of the real Postgres container. What's the likely cause and fix?
options: By default, @DataJpaTest auto-replaces the configured datasource with an embedded one, silently overriding the Testcontainers Postgres; adding @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE) disables that auto-replacement.
@DynamicPropertySource only takes effect when combined with @SpringBootTest, so switching from @DataJpaTest to @SpringBootTest is the only fix.
Testcontainers containers can only be injected into tests annotated @WebMvcTest, so the annotation choice itself is the mistake.
The PostgreSQLContainer must be declared non-static for @DynamicPropertySource to read its connection properties correctly.
explanation: The chapter calls this out explicitly as one of the most common 'why is my test still hitting H2' bugs — @DataJpaTest's embedded-database auto-configuration wins unless explicitly disabled.

promptText: A test suite has @DirtiesContext sprinkled across several test classes to fix intermittent failures. Why does the chapter call this a red flag rather than a fix?
options: @DirtiesContext forces Spring to rebuild the expensive cached application context, throwing away the caching benefit for every subsequent test class; using it to paper over a failure usually just hides the real bug — typically a singleton bean holding mutable state across tests — instead of fixing it.
@DirtiesContext is deprecated in modern Spring Boot and has no effect, so any test relying on it is actually still using the stale cached context.
@DirtiesContext only works when combined with @Transactional, so using it alone silently does nothing and the 'fix' is a placebo.
@DirtiesContext causes Testcontainers to skip starting a fresh container, which is why tests using real infrastructure appear to pass without truly testing anything.
explanation: This matches the chapter's Common Mistake callout — the annotation is a blunt, expensive tool that should prompt fixing the stateful singleton bean, not masking it.

promptText: The chapter describes a 'singleton container' pattern using a static initializer block that calls POSTGRES.start() but never calls .stop(). Why is it safe to never explicitly stop the container, and what mechanism actually cleans it up?
options: Testcontainers' Ryuk reaper process automatically detects and removes containers left running when the JVM/test run exits, so the container can be shared across every test class in the run without manual teardown.
It isn't actually safe — the chapter recommends this pattern only for local development, and in CI every container must be manually stopped in an @AfterAll method or the CI runner will crash.
PostgreSQLContainer automatically stops itself after 60 seconds of inactivity regardless of whether the JVM is still running, so no reaper is needed.
Docker itself refuses to let more than one container run per image, so leftover singleton containers are automatically terminated the next time a test suite starts.
explanation: The Ryuk reaper is Testcontainers' built-in cleanup mechanism, which is exactly what makes the 'start once, never stop explicitly' singleton pattern safe across the whole suite.

promptText: The chapter states a contract test needs only 'one service running at a time,' unlike an end-to-end test. Mechanically, how does Pact make this possible on the consumer side?
options: The consumer's Pact test starts an in-process mock HTTP server configured with the exact expected request/response interaction, and points the real client code at that mock server — so nothing about the consumer test requires the real provider to be running.
Pact automatically deploys a temporary copy of the real provider service into a Docker container during the consumer's test run, using the same image the provider team uses in production.
The consumer test replays previously recorded production traffic captured by a service mesh, removing the need for a live provider during the test.
Pact consumer tests only assert on request serialization, never on the response, which is why no server — mock or real — is needed on the consumer side.
explanation: The in-process mock server is the specific mechanism that decouples the consumer test from the provider's deploy schedule while still exercising the real client code against a realistic response.

promptText: A polyglot organization with independently-minded consumer teams is choosing between Pact and Spring Cloud Contract. Per the chapter, which factor should drive the decision, and which tool fits this scenario better?
options: The org's polyglot, consumer-independent shape favors Pact, since it is consumer-driven and language-agnostic, coordinated through a broker rather than requiring every service to be a Spring/JVM application.
Spring Cloud Contract fits better regardless of language mix, because its Groovy/YAML DSL can generate provider stubs for any language runtime with zero additional configuration.
The choice is purely stylistic since both tools are functionally identical in every respect, including which side (consumer or provider) authors the contract.
Pact should be avoided in polyglot orgs because its mock server only supports JVM-based consumers.
explanation: The chapter frames the decision around organizational shape — Pact's consumer-driven, language-agnostic model suits polyglot services with independent consumer teams, while Spring Cloud Contract's provider-driven model suits all-Spring shops.

promptText: Order Service's Pact test defines the provider state 'sku-1 has 5 units in stock' for a GET /inventory/sku-1 interaction. Inventory Service's CI then runs provider verification and later a can-i-deploy check before deploying. Explain how these two mechanisms work together to make the verification both deterministic and deploy-safe.
options: During verification, Pact invokes a registered state-handler that inserts the exact precondition data (e.g., saving that inventory record) right before replaying the recorded request against the real provider code — making the test deterministic without needing realistic seed data; can-i-deploy then separately queries the broker for whether every contract involving the specific versions about to be deployed is currently verified as compatible, blocking the deploy if not.

Provider states and can-i-deploy are two names for the same mechanism: the state-handler itself decides whether to allow the deploy, so a passing provider verification automatically triggers deployment with no separate broker query.

The provider state only matters for consumer-side tests, not provider verification, so Inventory Service's CI ignores state-handlers entirely and can-i-deploy instead re-runs the entire consumer test suite against the provider's staging environment.
can-i-deploy checks only whether the provider's unit tests pass; it has no relationship to Pact contracts or provider states, which exist solely to speed up test data setup.
explanation: Provider states manufacture exact preconditions on demand so verification isn't polluted by missing or stale seed data, while can-i-deploy is a distinct broker-side query about verification status of specific deployed versions in both directions — together they let independently-deployed teams ship safely without a shared release calendar.

promptText: A team's Pact contract asserts on the entire JSON response body verbatim, including fields the consumer never reads. Later, the provider adds a new optional field unrelated to anything the consumer uses, and verification fails. Combining the chapter's guidance on contract scope with its definition of backward-compatible changes, what's wrong and what's the fix?
options: Asserting on the full body over-specifies the contract beyond what the consumer depends on, so an unrelated additive change — which should be backward-compatible and invisible to a well-scoped contract — now fails verification; the fix is to match only the fields/status codes the consumer actually uses, with shape/type matchers instead of literal values where the exact value doesn't matter.

The failure is correct and expected behavior — any change to a provider's response, including adding unrelated fields, is always a breaking change under consumer-driven contract testing, so the provider must never add new fields once a contract exists.
The fix is to delete the contract and rely solely on the can-i-deploy check going forward, since contracts become unreliable once a provider's schema changes at all.
This failure indicates the consumer's mock server is misconfigured, not the contract's scope, so the fix is to regenerate the mock server rather than change what the contract asserts on.
explanation: This synthesizes two chapter points: verbatim full-body assertions are named as the most common way teams make contracts brittle, and adding an unused optional field is explicitly categorized as backward-compatible — something a properly-scoped contract shouldn't even notice.

promptText: Order Service needs to call Inventory Service's REST API. The chapter lays out a specific division of labor between WireMock, Testcontainers, and Pact for testing this outbound integration without ever deploying Inventory Service. What is that division, and why is a real Testcontainers instance of Inventory Service not part of it?
options: WireMock proves Order Service's own client code (retries, timeouts, deserialization, error handling) reacts correctly to controlled canned HTTP responses; Pact's consumer test proves those assumed responses actually match what the real Inventory Service will send. Testcontainers is reserved for dependencies whose real internal behavior matters (a database, a broker) — a REST API's value lies in its response shape, which WireMock plus Pact already cover without needing Inventory Service's real code running at all.

WireMock and Testcontainers are interchangeable for this scenario, so the chapter recommends running Inventory Service itself inside a Testcontainers GenericContainer and skipping Pact entirely, since a real running instance is always preferable to a contract.

Pact is used only to generate WireMock stub files automatically; the actual verification of correctness happens exclusively inside a Testcontainers-managed instance of Inventory Service, making WireMock and Pact redundant with each other.

Testcontainers cannot start REST APIs, only databases and brokers, which is a hard technical limitation — the chapter attributes the WireMock/Pact split entirely to this limitation rather than to a deliberate testing-strategy choice.
explanation: The chapter draws the split along 'does the dependency's real behavior matter' (Testcontainers: databases/brokers) versus 'do I just need to control response shape' (WireMock) versus 'is my assumed response shape actually correct' (Pact) — deliberately avoiding the need to run another team's real service at all.
